UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
 Midcontinent Independent System Operator,
                                                       Docket No. ER26-3650-000
 Inc.
               COMMENTS OF ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, LLC

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §
385.211, Rowan Digital Infrastructure, LLC ("Rowan") files these Comments, Request for
Clarification, and Limited Protest, to the August 28, 2026 filing by the Midcontinent Independent
System Operator, Inc. ("MISO") proposing Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads
(the "IRR Proposal") in Docket No. ER26-3650-000. Rowan supports MISO's objective of reliably
integrating large loads and requests targeted revisions to ensure that the obligations are clear,
workable, and predictable, appropriately aligned with operational control, and supported by
transparent compliance standards.

         I. COMPLIANCE RESPONSIBILITY SHOULD ALIGN WITH OPERATIONAL CONTROL
        Proposed Section 37A makes the Transmission Customer responsible for compliance.
Compliance responsibility should be assigned to the entity that owns, operates, or controls the
equipment, information, or operating function at issue. A Transmission Customer should not be held
responsible or subject to enforcement for a function controlled by MISO, a Transmission Owner, or
another entity, particularly where the Transmission Customer lacks the contractual or operational
authority necessary to perform that function.
         For Phasor Measurement Unit (“PMU”) equipment, proposed Section 37A.5 requires
installation by the Transmission Owner on its side of the Point of Withdrawal, at the Transmission
Customer’s expense; the equipment becomes part of the Transmission Owner’s interconnection
facilities, and the Transmission Owner provides the measurements to MISO. MISO should clarify that
PMU siting, quantity, installation, testing, maintenance, operation, and data delivery are the
Transmission Owner’s responsibilities, with cost responsibility addressed separately and any
Transmission Customer costs limited to documented, reasonable costs directly attributable to the PMU
facilities necessary to serve the applicable Large Load.

           II. MISO SHOULD CLARIFY MODELING AND MODIFICATION REQUIREMENTS
        Proposed Section 37A.2 requires verified electrical models and detailed Load profiles. MISO
should identify with specificity the required load-flow and stability models customarily provided
through interconnection studies, any additional model types, and the scope, format, granularity, and
timing of any required detailed Load profiles, and should avoid duplicative submissions. The Tariff
should also identify the applicable validation standard and distinguish information reasonably available
to the Transmission Customer from information controlled by customers, equipment manufacturers, or
other third parties.
        MISO should also define “material modifications,” using objective, reliability-based criteria,
establish specified and commercially reasonable review timelines, and limit prior approval to changes
that are reasonably expected to materially affect Transmission System reliability. Routine maintenance,
like-kind equipment replacement, and technology refreshes without such an effect should not be
delayed or subjected to prior approval. At a minimum, the Tariff should provide an expedited review
process and require MISO to identify the specific reliability concern supporting any denial or request
for additional information.

                                                   1
    III. FORECASTING REQUIREMENTS SHOULD REFLECT AVAILABLE OPERATING INFORMATION
       Proposed Section 37A.4 requires day-ahead and real-time Load Forecasts by the later of the
Service Commencement Date or September 1, 2027. New and expanding facilities may lack
representative operating history, and profiles may depend on tenant deployment, customer controlled
operating decisions, and phased energization.
        MISO should permit after-the-fact reporting where it satisfies the demonstrated reliability need.
If prospective forecasts are required, MISO should define the required forecast horizon, data format,
submission and accuracy standards, provide reasonable safe harbors during commissioning and phased
energization, defer representative Load-profile requirements until sufficient operating history exists,
and protect detailed operating data from unnecessary disclosure and limit its use to legitimate reliability
purposes. Forecast accuracy should be evaluated in light of the information reasonably available to the
Transmission Customer when the forecast is submitted, and good-faith forecast deviations should not
constitute a violation if the Transmission Customer used the applicable forecasting methodology and
the information reasonably available at the time.

      IV. RAMP REQUIREMENTS NEED A CLEAR BASIS AND SHOULD RECOGNIZE NET RAMP-
                                    SMOOTHING
       Proposed Section 37A.7 applies ramp limits during stable-state transitions, measured in
aggregate across applicable Points of Withdrawal, and allows eligible generation or other resources to
provide ramp smoothing. MISO proposes initial limits of 30 MW per minute.
        MISO should provide the technical and reliability basis for the proposed ramp limits and specify
the applicable measurement methodology, including the measurement interval, treatment of
measurement error, aggregation methodology, the circumstances constituting a stable state transition,
and how local planning criteria will be considered. MISO should also confirm that onsite battery energy
storage and other qualifying resources may provide ramp smoothing and that compliance will be
assessed on a net basis at the applicable Points of Withdrawal. Any site-specific limit should be based
on documented system conditions, provided to the affected Transmission Customer with the supporting
basis before it becomes enforceable, and accompanied by a reasonable implementation period.

V. RIDE-THROUGH REQUIREMENTS SHOULD COORDINATE WITH EXISTING PROTECTION SCHEMES
       Proposed Section 37A.6 requires Computational Load to remain connected during voltage and
frequency disturbances within criteria established in the Business Practice Manual. MISO should place
all material and operative performance criteria, measurement standards, exceptions, and compliance
pathways in the Tariff or otherwise subject them to Commission review before they become
enforceable. The Tariff should not permit a Business Practice Manual to create or materially expand a
Transmission Customer's substantive compliance obligations.
         MISO should explain how ride-through requirements will coordinate with approved under-
voltage and under-frequency load-shedding schemes, equipment protection settings, Transmission
Owner requirements, and other applicable reliability obligations. The framework should not require a
Computational Load to remain connected when shedding under an applicable protection scheme is the
reliability-supporting response, and compliance with an approved or required protection scheme should
not constitute a violation of Section 37A.6.

               VI. TRANSITION RELIEF SHOULD REFLECT ACTUAL PROJECT RELIANCE
        The proposal fully exempts the portion of a Large Load with a Service Commencement Date
on or before December 4, 2026. Loads meeting the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan/Expedited
Project Review (“MTEP/EPR”) Condition remain subject to Sections 37A.1 through 37A.5 and 37A.8

                                                    2
 but are exempt from Sections 37A.6 and 37A.7. Certain projects submitted for Expedited Project
Review from June 19 through October 31, 2026, may receive a waiver from Section 37A.6.
        Transition relief should also account for objective evidence of project maturity, reasonable
reliance, and binding commitments made before the Tariff’s effective date, including executed
interconnection, energy service, or transmission service agreements, material equipment procurement
commitments, completed engineering, and construction activities. Eligibility should not turn solely on
milestones controlled by a utility, MISO, or transmission provider, or on the timing of a third party's
processing or approval. The Tariff should identify the required waiver documentation, an objective
standard for approval, commercially reasonable review timelines, and written decision criteria. MISO
should also provide relief where compliance would require material redesign, replacement of
previously procured equipment, or impairment of binding pre-effective date commitments without a
demonstrated reliability necessity.

                                          VII. CONCLUSION

        Rowan respectfully requests that the Commission accept the IRR Proposal only subject to the
targeted revisions described above, including revisions necessary to align compliance responsibility
with operational control, establish objective and transparent compliance standards, coordinate
potentially conflicting reliability requirements, and provide reasonable transition relief for projects
undertaken in reliance on the existing framework.


Respectfully submitted,

ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, LLC

/s/ Tyler Petersen
Tyler Petersen
Director, Regulatory Affairs and Public Policy
1400 16th Street, Suite 330
Denver, Colorado 80202
